ety.text: From Middle French dérivatif, from Latin dērīvātus, perfect passive participle of dērīvō (“to derive”). Related to derive; by surface analysis, derive + -ative.

senses.d: Obtained by derivation; not radical, original, or fundamental.
Imitative of the work of someone else.
ex: No, I really felt it was very derivative. To me it it looked like it was straight out of Diane Arbus, but it had none of the wit.

senses.d: Referring to a work, such as a translation or adaptation, based on another work that may be subject to copyright restrictions.
Having a value that depends on an underlying asset of variable value.
Something derived.
A word formed by derivation, such as stylish from style.
A financial instrument whose value depends on the valuation of an underlying asset; such as a warrant, an option etc.
A chemical derived from another.

The derived function of f(x): the function giving the instantaneous rate of change of f; equivalently, the function giving the slope of the line tangent to the graph of f. Written f'(x) or (df)/(dx) in Leibniz's notation, ̇f(x) in Newton's notation (the latter used particularly when the independent variable is time).
ex: The derivative of x² is 2x; if f(x)#61;x², then f'(x)#61;2x

senses.d: The value of such a derived function for a given value of its independent variable: the rate of change of a function at a point in its domain.
ex: The derivative of f(x)#61;x³ at x#61;2 is 12.

senses.d: Any of several related generalizations of the derivative: the directional derivative, partial derivative, Fréchet derivative, functional derivative, etc.
The linear operator that maps functions to their derived functions, usually written D; the simplest differential operator.

ety.text: From Middle English deriven, from Old French deriver, from Latin dērīvō (“to lead, turn, or draw off (a liquid), draw off, derive”), from dē (“away”) + rīvus (“a stream”); see rival. Unrelated to arrive.

senses.d: To obtain or receive (something) from something else.
ex: Reading books is the best way to derive knowledge.

senses.d: To deduce (a conclusion) by reasoning.
To find the derivation of (a word or phrase).
To create (a compound) from another by means of a reaction.
To originate or stem (from).
ex: Her excellent organisation skills derive from her time as a secretary in the army.
Britannia's firebox would appear to have derived from those of the Bulleid Pacifics, which it closely resembles.

senses.d: To turn the course of (water, etc.); to divert and distribute into subordinate channels.
ex: For fear it [water] choke up the pits […] they [the workman] deriue it by other drains.

senses.d: To differentiate (a function).

Named after British executioner Thomas Derrick, who invented the framework arrangement commonly known by this name to aid in the conduct of executions. First use appears c. 1600 in the publication Ballad Death Earl Essex.

senses.d: A device that is used for lifting and moving large objects.
A framework that is constructed over a mine or oil well for the purpose of boring or lowering pipes.
An executioner responsible for hanging convicts; a hangman.
To hoist with, or as if with, a derrick.
To remove (a pitcher).
